statement.p: If \displaystyle L=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}, \ \ \frac {dx}{dt}=-1, \ \mbox{and } \frac {dy}{dt}=1, find \displaystyle\frac{dL}{dt} when x=2 and y=7.

solution.p: We rewrite L=(x^2+y^2)^\frac{1}{2} and then take the derivative of both sides with respect to t. \frac{dL}{dt}=\frac{1}{2}\left(x^2+y^2\right)^{\frac{-1}{2}}\left(2x \frac{dx}{dt}+2y\frac{dy}{dt}\right) Then we substitute what we know and solve for what we don't know. \frac{dL}{dt}=\frac{1}{2}\left(2^2+7^2\right)^{\frac{-1}{2}}\left(2\cdot2 \cdot -1+2\cdot7\cdot1\right)=0.686802819743445.
